title: The Painter's Voice
subtitle: Six months of hoarseness in a man who shouts for a living
description: Deciding when to examine the larynx, setting a baseline with a patient-reported measure, reading a perceptual profile, telling benign vocal fold lesions apart on stroboscopy, choosing the operative plane, and postoperative care.

steps.title: Step 1/6: When to Look at the Larynx
steps.scenario:
A 52-year-old house painter has been hoarse for six months. He works on active construction sites and shouts over compressor noise all day. He smokes half a pack daily and has done so for 20 years.

His primary care physician diagnosed reflux laryngitis and treated him with omeprazole 20 mg twice daily for eight weeks, then a methylprednisolone dose pack. Neither helped.

The larynx has never been examined. He has no dysphagia, no odynophagia, no otalgia and no weight loss. His neck is normal to palpation.
steps.question: What is your next step?

options.text: (A) Extend the proton pump inhibitor trial to 12 weeks with reflux precautions, then reassess
(B) Obtain a contrast-enhanced CT of the neck to exclude a mass before any endoscopy
(C) Perform laryngoscopy today
(D) Refer for voice therapy, and examine the larynx only if therapy fails

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

Six months of hoarseness in a current smoker, two empiric treatments already given, and the larynx never seen. The guideline allows laryngoscopy at any point in dysphonia and requires it if the voice has not improved within four weeks, or sooner when a serious cause is suspected. He passed both points months ago.

Why the others fail:
(A) The guideline recommends against antireflux medication for dysphonia alone when the larynx has not been examined. Eight weeks of twice-daily dosing has already failed, so extending it repeats the step rather than correcting it.
(B) The guideline recommends against CT or MRI before the larynx has been seen. Imaging costs money and radiation and does not show a mucosal lesion, which is what most dysphonia turns out to be.
(D) Voice therapy may well be the right treatment, but it comes after the diagnosis. The examination takes a few minutes and determines what the therapy is for.

On the steroid course: the guideline also advises against corticosteroids before the larynx is seen, partly because a short-lived response makes everyone more confident in a diagnosis that was never made.

Keypoint: empiric treatment estimates the cause; laryngoscopy establishes it.

Reference: Stachler RJ, Francis DO, Schwartz SR, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Hoarseness (Dysphonia) (Update). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42.

steps.title: Step 2/6: The Baseline Score
steps.scenario:
Before you examine him you have him complete the Voice Handicap Index-10. His total is 24 out of 40.

He tells you the voice is making it hard to direct his crew across a noisy site. You plan to repeat the score after treatment to judge the response.
steps.media: Load image: Completed VHI-10 form, interpretation bands cropped out. Caption: 'Voice Handicap Index-10.'
steps.question: What change in the total score counts as a minimal important difference in a general adult dysphonia population?

options.text: (A) 4 points
(B) 11 points
(C) No minimal important difference has been established; the score can only be reported as a severity band
(D) 6 points

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

The VHI-10 has 10 items scored 0 to 4, so the total runs 0 to 40. Misono studied 273 voice clinic patients and found that a change of 6 points matched a moderate change reported by the patient, while smaller changes could not be told apart from no change. On the Arffa normative bands (0-10 normal, 11-20 mild, 21-30 moderate, 31-40 severe), his 24 sits in the moderate range.

Why the others fail:
(A) 4 is a real published figure from the same research group, but it was derived in patients with vocal fold paralysis. A different population with a different baseline and a different treatment effect produces a different threshold, so the number does not carry across. An older consensus figure of 5 also circulates and predates any anchor-based work.
(B) 11 is the cutoff separating normal from mild on a single measurement. It describes who is abnormal, not who has changed.
(C) A minimal important difference does exist. Reporting only the band discards the instrument's ability to detect change within a band.

Keypoint: a cutoff tells you who is abnormal; a minimal important difference tells you who has improved.

Reference: Rosen CA, Lee AS, Osborne J, Zullo T, Murry T. Development and validation of the Voice Handicap Index-10. Laryngoscope. 2004;114(9):1549-1556. Misono S, Yueh B, Stockness AN, House ME, Marmor S. Minimal important difference in Voice Handicap Index-10. JAMA Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2017;143(11):1098-1103. Arffa RE, Krishna P, Gartner-Schmidt J, Rosen CA. Normative values for the Voice Handicap Index-10. J Voice. 2012;26(4):462-465. Young VN, Jeong K, Rothenberger SD, et al. Minimal clinically important difference of Voice Handicap Index-10 in vocal fold paralysis. Laryngoscope. 2018;128(6):1419-1424.

steps.title: Step 3/6: Listening to the Voice
steps.scenario:
You carry out a standard auditory-perceptual evaluation and record:

    G3    Overall grade, severe
    R2    Roughness, moderate
    B3    Breathiness, severe
    A1    Asthenia, slight
    S1    Strain, slight

A reference chart for the scale is on the wall.
steps.media: Load image: GRBASI reference chart. Caption: 'Perceptual scale.'
steps.question: Given this profile, what should you expect to find when you look?

options.text: (A) A unilateral lesion on the vibratory margin holding the folds apart and preventing complete closure
(B) Muscle tension dysphonia, with supraglottic compression and no lesion on the vibratory margin
(C) Bilateral vocal fold bowing from atrophy, with a spindle-shaped glottic gap
(D) Unilateral vocal fold paralysis, with an immobile fold and a wide glottic gap

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Read the whole profile rather than any single number. Severe breathiness means a lot of air is escaping. Moderate roughness means the two folds are vibrating unevenly. Asthenia and strain are both 1, so there is neither weakness nor excess effort. Air escaping without weakness and without strain means something is physically holding the folds apart while they vibrate, and the roughness adds asymmetry between the sides. That points to a mass on one vibratory margin.

Why the others fail:
(B) Muscle tension dysphonia comes from excessive laryngeal effort, so strain would be raised. It is 1. Strain is the parameter that separates hyperfunction from everything else.
(C) Atrophy gives a thin, weak voice, so asthenia would rise alongside breathiness. Asthenia is 1. Both atrophy and a mass cause breathiness, and weakness is what tells them apart.
(D) Paralysis also causes marked breathiness, but the glottic gap is inefficient, so it usually brings reduced loudness and raised asthenia with it. Asthenia of 1 argues against it, and fold mobility on the next examination will settle it.

On the chart: the version shown is the extended GRBASI scale, which adds Instability for change in voice quality over time. Classic GRBAS uses the five parameters above, each rated 0 normal to 3 severe. Record all five, because leaving out the normal ones discards exactly the findings that rule out the other three answers here.

Keypoint: one raised parameter names the sound; the pattern across all five names the cause.

Reference: Hirano M. Clinical Examination of Voice. Springer-Verlag; 1981. Yamauchi EJ, Imaizumi S, Maruyama H, Haji T. Perceptual evaluation of pathological voice quality: a comparative analysis between the RASATI and GRBASI scales. Logoped Phoniatr Vocol. 2010;35:121-128.

steps.title: Step 4/6: What the Stroboscope Shows
steps.scenario:
You perform laryngoscopy with stroboscopy.

There is a single translucent exophytic lesion on the left vocal fold, at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds. The right fold is smooth. Both folds move fully. Glottic closure is incomplete with an hourglass shape around the lesion. The mucosal wave is present and symmetric, including across the lesion itself.
steps.media: Load video: Videostroboscopy of the larynx during phonation, unannotated. 10 seconds, muted. Caption: 'Stroboscopy.'
steps.question: Which diagnosis fits these findings?

options.text: (A) Vocal fold nodules: bilateral symmetric lesions at the mid-membranous point, usually responding to voice therapy alone
(B) Reinke's edema: diffuse polypoid change across the full membranous length of both folds, strongly smoking-related, lowering habitual pitch
(C) Vocal fold polyp: unilateral, translucent or hemorrhagic and exophytic, with the mucosal wave usually preserved, and responding poorly to voice therapy alone
(D) Intracordal cyst: a subepithelial encapsulated lesion, usually with a reduced mucosal wave over the lesion and often a reactive lesion opposite it

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

Solitary, unilateral, translucent and exophytic, with the mucosal wave preserved across the lesion and an hourglass closure defect. The lesion sits superficially and does not tether the deeper layers, so the wave continues. The hourglass gap explains the severe breathiness heard in Step 3. Polyps usually do not resolve with voice therapy alone, which is why the earlier medical treatment failed and why surgery is now worth discussing, with voice therapy alongside it to deal with the shouting that produced the lesion.

Why the others fail:
(A) Nodules are bilateral and roughly symmetric and sit at the mid-membranous point, where impact stress is greatest. They are also the lesion that does respond to voice therapy. A single exophytic lesion is not a nodule.
(B) Reinke's edema is diffuse rather than focal and involves the whole membranous fold on both sides. Its usual complaint is a dropped pitch, which he does not describe. His smoking history makes this feel like the answer, and the distribution rules it out.
(D) Cyst against polyp is the discrimination that changes the operation, and the mucosal wave is what separates them. A cyst sits under the epithelium, tethers the cover, and reduces the wave over the lesion. Here the wave is preserved and symmetric.

Keypoint: appearance suggests the diagnosis; the mucosal wave decides it.

Reference: Hirano M. Morphological structure of the vocal cord as a vibrator and its variations. Folia Phoniatr (Basel). 1974;26(2):89-94. Note: the stroboscopic features separating polyp, nodule, Reinke's edema and cyst rest on consensus description rather than on a single trial.

steps.title: Step 5/6: In the Operating Room
steps.scenario:
After counseling he elects surgery.

You have completed a subepithelial infusion and are planning the epithelial incision.
steps.media: Load image: Microlaryngoscopic view of the left vocal fold with the lesion in the operative field, unannotated. Caption: 'Microlaryngoscopy.'
steps.question: Which technique is correct, and why?

options.text: (A) Excise the lesion with a margin of surrounding normal mucosa, so that no microscopic residual lesion is left
(B) Incise the epithelium immediately lateral to the lesion, dissect within the superficial lamina propria to deliver it, then redrape the preserved epithelium
(C) Carry the dissection down to the vocal ligament and thyroarytenoid muscle, so that any submucosal component is fully excavated
(D) Ablate the lesion with the CO2 laser, which is hemostatic and avoids handling a specimen

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

Hirano described the vocal fold as three mechanical layers: the cover, meaning the epithelium and superficial lamina propria, which produces the mucosal wave; the transition, meaning the vocal ligament; and the body, meaning the thyroarytenoid muscle. Scar in the superficial lamina propria cannot be reversed. So the incision goes lateral to the lesion, the dissection stays in the most superficial plane that will deliver it, and the epithelium is redraped rather than removed. Send the specimen: he is a current smoker, and keratosis or dysplasia can look exophytic.

Why the others fail:
(A) Taking a margin of normal mucosa is cancer surgery applied to a benign lesion. It removes working vibratory tissue and gains nothing.
(C) Dissecting to the ligament turns a cover problem into a body injury, and it reliably produces scar and permanent hoarseness.
(D) Ablation destroys the specimen, so there is no histology, and it delivers heat to the layer you most need to protect. Vocal cord stripping was the same mistake on a larger scale and was abandoned for the same reason.

Keypoint: remove the lesion and keep the cover, because scar in the superficial lamina propria cannot be undone.

Reference: Hirano M. Morphological structure of the vocal cord as a vibrator and its variations. Folia Phoniatr (Basel). 1974;26(2):89-94. Note: the microflap technique rests on phonosurgical technique literature and consensus rather than on a single randomized trial.

steps.title: Step 6/6: Before He Goes Home
steps.scenario:
Surgery is uneventful. The lesion is removed and the flap is well redraped. Histopathology returns a benign vocal fold polyp with subepithelial edema and no dysplasia.

You see him before discharge.
steps.question: What do you plan and what do you tell him?

options.text: (A) Complete voice rest for four weeks, nothing by mouth for 72 hours, and antibiotics to protect the healing margin
(B) No voice restriction and immediate return to full duties, since the lesion was benign and completely excised
(C) Complete voice rest for about three days, plus a routine proton pump inhibitor and a corticosteroid taper
(D) Complete voice rest for about three days, then graduated voice use with speech-language pathology, hydration, smoking cessation support, and work on vocal load at the job site

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

Voice rest is one of the few questions here with randomized data behind it, and the data do not favor longer rest. Kaneko randomized microflap patients to three or seven days of complete rest and found that three days followed by early voice therapy gave better recovery of vibratory function at six months. Fan compared seven days of complete rest against three days complete plus four days relative rest and found similar improvement at one month. Early controlled use appears to favor organized healing over scar.

The behavioral side matters as much as the surgery. The lesion came from shouting across a noisy site, and the operation does not change that exposure.

Why the others fail:
(A) Four weeks of silence is contradicted by the trials above, and long rest causes deconditioning, compensatory muscle tension, and poor adherence. Nothing by mouth and routine antibiotics have no role.
(B) Goes too far the other way and drops both the graduated return and the vocal load management that prevents a recurrence.
(C) The voice rest part is right, which is what makes this feel correct. Routine acid suppression and a steroid taper for every patient repeat the Step 1 problem of treating without an indication. He has no reflux findings and no reason for steroids.

Two things to say before surgery rather than after: suspension can cause temporary tongue numbness or altered taste, usually settling within a month, and a small number of patients get no improvement while a few are worse. Repeating the VHI-10 closes the loop from Step 2, where a fall of six points or more counts as a meaningful response.

Keypoint: short voice rest with early therapy beats long silence, and behavior change is what prevents the next polyp.

Reference: Kaneko M, Shiromoto O, Fujiu-Kurachi M, Kishimoto Y, Tateya I, Hirano S. Optimal duration for voice rest after vocal fold surgery: randomized controlled clinical study. J Voice. 2017;31(1):97-103. Fan RS, Yiu Y, Kulesz PA, et al. Clinical voice outcomes for two voice rest protocols after phonomicrosurgery. Laryngoscope. 2024;134(6):2812-2818.
